tagline.text: A coral snorkeling marine reserve around seven rocky islets just off Coron town

location.label: Location
location.text: Coron, Palawan; coast east of Coron town toward Maquinit, around seven small rocky islets in the sea

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,200 (per person, based on entry, boat or kayak, and a round-trip tricycle)

children.text: Siete Pecados is a marine reserve 20–30 minutes from Coron town by tricycle, where you snorkel on the coral reefs around seven small limestone islets. Because it rarely appears on island-hopping itineraries, it makes an easy half-day trip of its own from town.

Siete Pecados is Spanish for "Seven Sins." The name refers to seven small limestone islets lying off Coron town, and the waters around them form a marine reserve. According to a local legend, seven sisters who defied their parents and played in the sea were swept away by the waves, and seven islets rose overnight where they vanished. Details of the legend differ from source to source, so it is fun to hear it from a local guide.
The reserve was created in 2005 on the proposal of the local community. Its protected area is said to be about
1.8 km²

, and it safeguards not only coral reefs but also mangrove forests and seagrass beds. It belongs to the Calamianes Island marine protected area network, and part of it is a no-take zone where fishing is banned. Residents began protecting the sea after dynamite and cyanide fishing damaged it around 1998, and today locals guide visitors, patrol the area and earn a living from it. The park manager said in a 2024 press interview that 60% of the park's income goes to conservation, with the remaining 40% split between the city of Coron and the barangay. This comes from a single news report that other sources have not confirmed, and the shares may change over time, so treat it as a rough guide.

The results have been recognized. Coral cover is higher than outside the reserve and has increased since it was established, and it is described as having the highest fish species richness and fish biomass in the Calamianes marine protected areas. In April 2024 the Marine Conservation Institute in the United States named it a Blue Park. Threatened marine life reported here includes hawksbill sea turtles, dugongs, humphead wrasse and Pectinia maxima, a coral endemic to the region.

For travelers, easy access is the biggest advantage. Coron's famous island tours mean a long boat ride, but Siete Pecados is reached overland from town and then a short paddle. Most big island tours skip it, so it fits well on an afternoon when you are tired of touring or on a free half day. It suits families and beginners who want to snorkel slowly in shallow water, and paddling a kayak yourself is part of the fun. You can have breakfast at your hotel in town and be back before lunch, so if you stay in Coron two days or more it works well as a rest-day activity. Rather than expecting spectacular coral walls or shipwrecks, go for the calm sea of the reserve and the coral the community has nurtured, and you will be more satisfied.

In the shallow water around the islets you can see brain coral, staghorn coral, table coral, mushroom coral and more. It is not astonishingly colorful, but as a reserve the coral is in good condition and the water is clear on many days. Snorkel gear is enough; no scuba is needed. In the shallow parts, even weak swimmers can wear a life vest and simply put their faces in, so it is a good place for a child's first snorkel.

You can see clownfish, parrotfish, butterflyfish, triggerfish, lionfish, damselfish, angelfish, groupers and more. Sea cucumbers, starfish and sea urchins sit on the bottom, and with luck a sea turtle passes by. Guides lead you along paths between the coral rather than over it. Even on days when the water looks murky, small fish gather close to the islets, and chasing them with your eyes is a pleasure.
If you rent a kayak, it takes about
5–10 minutes

to paddle from the landing to the islets. When the waves are calm, even beginners find it easy. You tie the kayak to a mooring buoy or the pier before entering the water, and no anchors are dropped, so the coral is not harmed.
A boat usually carries 2–4 people and a captain guides you. Life vests are provided, and the trip takes about
2 hours
. The guide goes into the water with you and points out what to see, so you can feel safe even if you are not a strong swimmer.

Besides coral reefs, the reserve includes mangrove forest and seagrass beds. Near the shore there is also a route where you paddle a kayak through the mangroves, which is a pleasant way to enjoy the scenery on the water. The seagrass beds are feeding grounds for protected species such as dugongs, so do not stand on or stir up the bottom when you enter the water.

Maquinit Hot Springs lies on the same road, and visiting both in one afternoon is popular. After snorkeling, rinse off the salt water in the hot springs and the day ends well. Check the hot spring's fees and opening hours locally.

blocks.title: A sea protected by the community

children.text: Local guards watch over the area in shifts by day and night. Your visitor fees go to conservation and local livelihoods, so rather than haggling, pay the set fee and follow your guide's instructions.
Leave Coron town by tricycle for the Siete Pecados tourist information office. If you agree on waiting time and book a round trip, it is easier to get a ride back.
At the office, choose your entry, boat or kayak, and gear, and pick up a life vest and mask. The sea is calmest in the morning when the wind is weak.
Head out to the islets by kayak or boat and snorkel among the coral for about an hour and a half.
Return to the landing, check whether showers and snacks are available, and catch your breath. Some reviews say there is no toilet, so use one beforehand.
Move on to Maquinit Hot Springs, or return to town for lunch.
It gets crowded and the sun is strong at midday, so a morning visit is better. If you go in the afternoon, get into the water by 3 PM at the latest.

items.title: Afternoon course
items.subtitle: A relaxed hour after an island tour

children.text: Have lunch in town, then call a tricycle and set out.
Rent a kayak and snorkel gear at the office.
Snorkel for about an hour and paddle around the edges of the islets by kayak.
Head back to town before the sun gets low. Many sources give the park's closing time as 4 PM, so do not leave it late.
Opening hours differ between sources, so check with the office first.
There are direct flights from Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Francisco B. Reyes Airport (USU) in Busuanga. Check airlines and schedules when you book.
From the airport to Coron town you travel by van or taxi. Check fares locally.

You can also fly from Manila to Puerto Princesa and continue to Coron by land or sea, but it often takes more than a day. Only recommend it to travelers with time to spare; on a short trip, taking the direct Manila–Busuanga flight is better. Check timetables and fares for each leg locally.
From town to the Siete Pecados tourist information office is on the same road as Maquinit Hot Springs and takes about
20–30 minutes
, partly on an unpaved dirt road.
One review paid
for a round trip including an hour of waiting, another reported a
round trip, and another guide gave around
. Fares vary widely, so agree before leaving, including the number of people and waiting time.
It is hard to find a tricycle for the return. Ask the driver to wait and agree on the extra hourly charge in advance.
The Google Maps pin sits on the water and can make navigation confusing. Tell the driver "Siete Pecados tourist information office" as your destination.
Pay the entry fee at the office and choose a boat or a kayak. The islets are
5–10 minutes
away by kayak.
Many guides say no reservation is needed, and the wait is usually short.

The dry season from November to May is best for snorkeling in Coron, when the sea is calm and visibility is good. The reserve is open all year, but in the rainy season wind and rain can make entering the water difficult and the office may be closed on some days, so check the latest notices.
Even on the same day, the water is calmest and the crowds smallest in the morning. At midday the wind picks up and visitors increase.

Siete Pecados is a day trip from town, so there is no need to stay nearby. Coron town is the most convenient base, and there are resorts on the seaside. If you want to get into the water early in the morning, a town hotel is better for getting there. If you have a spare day, plan the morning at Siete Pecados and the afternoon at the town market and a walk along the waterfront.

There are almost no restaurants or facilities near the park, and no ATM. Eat lunch in town before going, or bring snacks and water. Carry plenty of cash. One review suggests asking at the office whether coconuts are sold after your visit.
A local guide recommends bringing your own snorkel gear. Some say rental on site has a narrow selection and costs more.
Bring cash and small change. There is no ATM nearby and card payment may be hard.
Do not touch or step on the coral, and follow the route set by your guide. Coral damage is the biggest problem.
Use reef-safe sunscreen or wear a rash guard.
Pack a dry bag, water shoes, a dry towel, a hat, sunglasses, water and snacks.
If you kayak yourself, you can leave paddles and bags on the pier, but keep valuables in a dry bag on your body.
Going in the morning means a calm sea, fewer people and better visibility.
A waterproof camera or action cam is good for taking underwater photos.
When you agree on waiting time with the tricycle driver, mention the number of people and bags to reduce fare disputes.
Before entering the water, note the direction of the islets and the landing you will return to, so you do not lose your bearings.
Fees and opening hours differ between sources and must be confirmed locally. Treat the amounts in this guide only as approximate ₱ ranges.
Some reviews say there is no toilet, so use one before you leave.
You may meet a sea snake in the water. Do not panic; keep your distance and back away calmly.
Kayaking is not safe on days with strong wind and currents. Follow the office staff first and always wear a life vest.
Do not touch marine life or coral or leave trash. Fishing is prohibited.
The road is unpaved and the tricycle shakes a lot. Prepare in advance if you get motion sickness.
Coron
town is
20–30 minutes
away by tricycle, so you can base your meals and lodging in town and visit from there.
Twin Lagoon (Coron)
is a lagoon entered between limestone cliffs from the sea and a signature stop on island tours.
A clear lake below limestone cliffs,
Kayangan Lake
is often visited on Coron island tours.
A natural hot spring on the road to Siete Pecados. Check fees and hours locally.
